# Locality Guide: Ohio, United States (ca. 1788–1803, Pre-Statehood Northwest Territory)

## Jurisdiction Overview

In 1790, Ohio was **not yet a state** — it was part of the Northwest Territory, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Ohio became the first state carved from that territory in **1803**. The administrative center was **Washington County** (organized 1788), the first county in the territory; **Hamilton County** followed in 1790.

---

## Boundary Changes

Boundary changes in this era were **frequent and significant**. Washington County (1788) originally covered a vast area; Hamilton County was organized in 1790 from the remainder. Any ancestor in "Ohio" in 1790 was legally in one of these two enormous counties (or unorganized territory). Their boundaries were repeatedly redrawn as new counties were carved out through statehood and beyond — so researchers must determine **which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event**, not assume today's county lines apply.

> Per the FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio Genealogy," Northwest Territory and Boundary Changes section: "Boundary changes were frequent — researchers must determine which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event."

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- No statewide birth/death registration existed in 1790.
- **Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013** (FamilySearch collection 1803785, ~3M people) begins right at the edge of this period — pre-1803 county marriage records *may* exist for Washington/Hamilton counties.
- **Ohio, County Death Records** (collection 1417891) only starts in **1840** — a confirmed gap for 1790.
- **Alternatives:** Church records and county marriage registers.

### Church Records
- **Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950** (FamilySearch collection 2246917, ~678K people) covers 1790 directly. This is a primary substitute for missing civil vital registration.

### Census Records
- The **1790 federal census did not cover the Northwest Territory** — it was not yet organized as a state or listed territory in that enumeration. The 1790–1800 period is effectively a **federal census gap** for this area.
- **Alternative:** Use tax lists in place of census records.

### Land Records
Two overlapping, historically distinct land-grant systems operated here:
- **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers): reserved for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans, surveyed by metes and bounds. Warrants held at the **Virginia State Library**.
- **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio): surveyed on a rectangular grid. Records held at the **Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland**.
- **FamilySearch:** "Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840" (collection 1542187, ~234K people) covers 1790.
- A browse-only volume of **Territorial Land Records, Northwest Territory, 1788–1799** (image group 005112233, 51 images, 0% indexed) exists — must be browsed image by image.

### Tax Records
- **Washington County, Ohio tax volume, 1799–1803** (image group 005112240, 73 images, 12% name-indexed) — a key substitute for the missing 1790–1800 federal census.
- **Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850** (FamilySearch collection 1987542, ~345K people) begins just after the target period.

### Military Records
- Bounty-land warrant records tied to Revolutionary War service are likely relevant (given the Virginia Military District), but no specific collection was confirmed in this search. Try the **National Archives (NARA)** for service, pension, and bounty-land records.

### Probate and Court Records
- Early Washington and Hamilton County court records are the expected custodians, but no online collection was found in this survey — treat these as **physical-repository-only** until confirmed otherwise.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church records (1787+), county marriages (1789+), land records (1787+), tax records (1800+) | Free |
| Virginia State Library | Virginia Military District land warrants | In-person / mail |
| Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland | Connecticut Western Reserve land records | In-person / mail |
| Ohio History Connection, Columbus | Early territorial court and land records | In-person / request |
| County courthouses (Washington, Hamilton) | Deeds, probate, court minute books | In-person / mail |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal land, military, court records | Free (originals by request) |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery/burial records | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Determine county jurisdiction first.** Pin down whether your ancestor's location fell under Washington County or Hamilton County before searching county-level records — the boundary lines shifted repeatedly.

2. **Identify the land-grant district** (Virginia Military District vs. Connecticut Western Reserve vs. general federal public land) before choosing a land-records repository — each has a different custodian and survey system.

3. **Use tax lists as a census substitute.** The 1790–1800 federal census gap for this area makes early tax lists (especially the Washington County volume, 1799–1803) an essential alternative.

4. **Church records are your primary vital record source.** Civil registration did not exist. The FamilySearch "Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950" collection (2246917) covers this period directly.

5. **Some early volumes are browse-only** (0% indexed). The territorial land records volume (1788–1799) must be paged through image by image.

6. **Consult the live FamilySearch Wiki directly** for Ohio-specific pages on vital records, land records, census, and church records — several specific Ohio Wiki pages returned only generic content in this search and could not be confirmed with detail here.

---

**Bottom line:** Ohio in 1790 was raw frontier territory under the Northwest Ordinance, with just two enormous and frequently-redrawn counties. There was no census coverage and no civil vital registration, but church registers (1787+), county marriage records (1789+), land records tied to two special grant systems, and early tax lists fill most of the gap. The most critical first step is pinpointing which county — Washington or Hamilton — governed the specific location, and which land-grant district it fell within, before choosing where to search.

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1860, Gold Rush Era)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Statehood:** California became a U.S. state in **1850**, bypassing territorial status entirely.
- **Key hubs:** San Francisco and Sacramento were the principal boomtowns.
- **Context:** Roughly 300,000 migrants arrived between 1848–1855, drawn by gold discovered at Sutter's Mill on January 24, 1848. The population was transient, predominantly male, and highly diverse in origin.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **California, County Births, 1850–1919** — FamilySearch collection 2017276 (~789,000 persons), held at the county level.
- **California, County Marriages, 1850–1952** — FamilySearch collection 1452832 (~1.1 million persons), county level.
- **Pre-statehood alternative:** Franciscan mission registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) covered 1769–1850 → **California, Mission Records, 1769–1850** (FamilySearch collection 1804372, ~99,000 persons; records generally in Spanish).

### Census Records
- **1850 Federal Census** — the first taken in California, but some county returns are **missing or partially destroyed**; essential but incomplete.
- **California State Census, 1850–1852** — FamilySearch image group 006601001 (88% name-indexed, full-text searchable); a valuable substitute where the federal census has gaps.

### Mining & Land Records
- **Mining Claim Registers, San Francisco, 1849–1855** — FamilySearch image group 006601002 (340 images, **0% indexed, browse-only**). Must be examined page by page; no name search available.
- General land patents in federal land states route through the **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov), though California-specific detail was not confirmed by this survey's tools.

### Immigration / Passenger Records
- **Ship passenger manifests, San Francisco** — held at **NARA, San Bruno** (National Archives, San Francisco Bay Area). Examine the full manifest, not just name indexes, as children frequently appear unindexed.
- **Port Arrival Registers, Sacramento, 1849–1858** — FamilySearch image group 006601003 (298 images, **0% indexed, browse-only**).

### Later Settlement Records (Post–Gold Rush)
- **California, Great Registers, 1866–1910** — FamilySearch collection 1923340 (~1.3 million persons; voter registration). Begins in 1866 — documents those who *stayed*, not the initial 1848–1855 wave; useful for tracking a miner's settled years.

### Church Records
- Franciscan Catholic mission records are the primary pre-1850 vital-event source (see Mission Records collection above).
- No Gold Rush–era Protestant or other denominational collections were returned by this survey's tools — treat as a coverage gap, not confirmed absence.

### Other Record Types (Not Confirmed Online)
- Probate, court, and tax records are held at the county courthouse level; no specific California collection was confirmed by tools in this survey.
- Cemetery, newspaper, and military record collections specific to this era were not returned by tools; use the external repositories listed below as starting points.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | County births/marriages 1850+; Mission Records; State Census 1850–52; Mining Claim Registers; Port Arrival Registers; Great Registers 1866+ | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census collection (supplements the partially destroyed 1850 CA census) | Subscription |
| **NARA Online (Fold3 / Archives.gov)** | Military records; San Francisco passenger manifests | Free / Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery records | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical California newspapers | Subscription |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Archives, San Bruno (NARA Pacific Region)** | Ship passenger manifests, San Francisco arrivals | In-person / mail |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Gold Rush–era manuscripts, overland trail diaries, journals | In-person |
| **California State Library** | Gold Rush–era manuscript collections | In-person |
| **County Courthouses** | Probate, land, mining claim originals | In-person / mail |

---

## Known Record Losses
Some 1850 federal census county returns for California are reported as missing or partially destroyed. The **California State Census, 1850–1852** (FamilySearch image group 006601001) is the most practical substitute — it is 88% indexed and full-text searchable.

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1850-52 state census** as a supplement whenever the federal census shows gaps for a particular California county.
2. **Mining Claim Registers and Port Arrival Registers on FamilySearch are browse-only** (0% indexed) — budget time for image-by-image review; there is no name search shortcut.
3. **San Francisco passenger manifests at NARA San Bruno** are critical for documenting a migrant's arrival by sea — examine the full page, not just the index.
4. **Mission Records** (1769–1850) are for families already in California before the Gold Rush, not for the migrants themselves, but they document any California-born women a miner may have married.
5. **Great Registers** (1866+) can confirm that a miner stayed and settled after the rush, and may record birthplace, nativity, and physical description — excellent for linking to earlier records.
6. **Bancroft Library and California State Library** hold unique unpublished materials (diaries, letters, overland journals) not digitized online — worth contacting directly for a forty-niner ancestor.
7. The FamilySearch catalog returned zero hits for California in this survey, which is a cataloguing gap — check the FamilySearch Catalog directly for microfilm holdings not yet surfaced here.

---

This guide covers what the survey's tools confirmed. For a specific county (e.g., El Dorado, Calaveras, Tuolumne — the heart of the Mother Lode), a county-level locality guide would add boundary history and more precise record-set details. A research-plan agent can then turn these record types into a sequenced search plan for a named ancestor.

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California became a U.S. state in 1850, bypassing territorial status (per Wikipedia summary of the California Gold Rush).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Varies by county; San Francisco and Sacramento were the chief boomtowns of the era.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States (statehood 1850).
- **Population during period:** `place_population` returned no data for California, United States for 1848–1860 — this survey could not confirm population figures from that tool.
- **Economy:** Gold mining dominated 1848–1855, driving a massive, transient, predominantly male migration (Wikipedia, "California Gold Rush").
- **Ethnic composition:** Migrants came from diverse origins across the U.S. and abroad (Wikipedia).
- **Religious denominations:** Franciscan mission-era Catholic records predate statehood; later Gold Rush-era denominations are not detailed in the sources retrieved.
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill, January 24, 1848; roughly 300,000 migrants arrived; statehood in 1850 (Wikipedia).

## Boundary changes
This survey did not confirm county-level boundary changes within 1848–1860; California's counties were newly organized at statehood. A researcher narrowing to a specific county should request a county-level locality guide for boundary history.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York — Colonial Period (1700s)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Origin:** New York City began as the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam (1624), seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York.
- **Governing jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British colonial administration through 1783); New York State was not formed until 1788.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed, Anglican (Trinity Church), and Presbyterian churches kept extensive records in this period.
- **Key historical events:** Dutch-to-British transfer of control in 1664; NYC served as the provincial capital throughout the colonial era.

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York, United States (1700–1783, British colonial period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New York City dates from 1624 as the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam, seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York (Wikipedia, "New York City").
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City itself was the provincial capital of the Province of New York through much of the colonial era.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British colonial administration); the modern state of New York was formed in 1788 per `place_search` (`standardPlace: "New York, United States"`, dateRange `+1788/`).
- **Population during period:** `place_population` returned no data for "New York, New York, United States" for 1700–1800 — this survey could not confirm population figures for the target window.
- **Economy:** Major commercial port and administrative center under British rule (Wikipedia).
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed, Anglican (Trinity Church), and Presbyterian churches kept extensive records (Wikipedia; FamilySearch Wiki search result, "New York City Genealogy" — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Key historical events:** Dutch-to-British transfer of control in 1664; the city served briefly as the first U.S. capital after the colonial period ended (Wikipedia).

## Boundary changes
- The colony transitioned from Dutch (New Amsterdam, to 1664) to British administration (New York, 1664–1783); records from the Dutch period and early British period form one continuous trail and should be searched together rather than as separate record sets.
- New York State as a jurisdiction was not formed until 1788, after the period of interest — during the 1700s, governance was at the provincial level.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** This survey found no FamilySearch Wiki page specifically for New York City or New York State vital records start dates — repeated `wiki_read` attempts for `New_York_City_Vital_Records` and `New_York_Vital_Records` both resolved to a generic "Genealogy_Records" page with no jurisdiction-specific date. No level or year can be confirmed from this survey.
- **What exists:** No civil vital registration system is documented for this period by the tools used; church registers served this function (see below).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers — see Church records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous series, beginning 1639 per the FamilySearch Wiki search result), Anglican (Trinity Church), and Presbyterian (FamilySearch Wiki search, "New York City Genealogy" — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials.
- **Where held:** `volume_search` found one digitized volume directly on point: image group 007733180, 211 images, covering "New York City, New York, United States," 1700–1776, record type "Dutch Reformed Church Registers," language Dutch (`nl`). It is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — browse-only, and in the Dutch language, so the researcher must read the original Dutch text image by image. `collections_search` separately lists "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (collection id 1469062, 2,345,678 persons) at the state scope.
- **Gaps:** This survey's `catalog_search` for both "New York, New York, United States" and "New York, United States" returned 0 hits — a cataloguing gap for microfilm/manuscript holdings of these church registers; report this as a gap, not evidence the registers don't exist.
- **Language:** The Dutch Reformed registers (1700–1776) are in Dutch — translation/reading skill in Dutch is needed.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Not applicable until 1790 (post-dates most of the colonial period); the FamilySearch generic guide page confirms federal census begins 1790.
- **Other enumerations:** No colonial-era NYC enumeration was confirmed by any tool in this survey.
- **Access:** Not established by this survey for the 1700s window.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianship files. The FamilySearch Wiki search result notes wills proved before the Prerogative Court of New York are indexed in the "Abstracts of Wills" series published by the New-York Historical Society (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records).
- **Date range:** `collections_search` lists "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (id 1542780, 987,654 persons) — this date range covers the full 1700s.
- **Where held:** Per the wiki search result, abstracts are published by the New-York Historical Society; FamilySearch holds a digitized collection.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not determinable without a specific ancestor; search both wills (testate) and administrations (intestate).

### Land records
- **Types:** Land conveyances/patents (Wikipedia). `collections_search` lists "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (id 2078654, 1,567,890 persons), covering the 1700s.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not stated by any FamilySearch Wiki page retrieved in this survey (both jurisdiction-specific vital/land pages resolved to the generic template) — this survey did not confirm the colonial land-granting office.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch digitized collection noted above; no county courthouse detail confirmed for this period.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Colonial militia; FamilySearch Wiki search result notes the Province of New York maintained militia rolls listing men of military age (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records).
- **Record types:** Militia rolls.
- **Where held:** Not specified by tool results beyond the above note.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Tax assessment lists. The wiki search result states tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards during the colonial period. `collections_search` separately lists "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (id 1678432, 123,456 persons) — this collection's date range (1799–1804) is at the tail end of, and slightly after, the 1700s window; useful as a bridge but not covering most of the century.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for the absence of any 18th-century census.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York was a major colonial port; no specific port-of-entry passenger-list collection for the 1700s was returned by any tool in this survey.

### Newspaper records
- Wikipedia names the New York Gazette as a colonial-era newspaper; no FamilySearch collection or external link specific to it was returned by the tools used.

### Cemetery records
- `external_links_search` returned Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) as a general cemetery-record resource; no NYC-specific colonial cemetery collection was returned.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (id 1469062); "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (id 2078654); "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (id 1542780); "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (id 1678432); digitized Dutch Reformed Church Registers volume (image group 007733180, 1700-1776) | Absence of civil vital registration in this period | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Post-1790 census coverage only; does not reach the colonial period | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Militia/service record gap | Subscription (per external_links_search listing) |
| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ | Federal-level military and later immigration records | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` for 1700–1799 returned exactly one matching digitized volume (the Dutch Reformed Church Registers, image group 007733180); no `nextPageToken` was present, so this appears to be the complete matching set for that query, not a partial page.

### Physical repositories
No physical repository (archive, historical society, courthouse) was named with holdings detail by any tool in this survey beyond the FamilySearch Wiki search's mention that the New York Genealogical & Biographical Society and the New-York Historical Society hold extensive colonial-era collections (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records). No address, hours, or access method was returned for either.

## Records NOT online
The 0%-indexed, non-full-text-searchable Dutch Reformed Church Registers (1700–1776, image group 007733180) exist only as browse-only page images in Dutch — there is no name search into them. `catalog_search` returned 0 hits for microfilm/manuscript holdings at both the city and state level, so this survey could not confirm what, if anything, of the colonial probate, land, tax, or court record originals is held in any physical repository, or where.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that any New York City colonial-era record series was destroyed or lost. This is not confirmation of survival — it is simply outside what was checked; no claim either way should be made beyond what is stated here.

## Research tips
- Search the Dutch Reformed Church Registers (1700–1776) image by image — they are 0% indexed and in Dutch (volume_search, image group 007733180).
- Also check the Anglican (Trinity Church) and Presbyterian registers named in the FamilySearch Wiki search result, since FamilySearch's own church-records collection (id 1469062) spans 1640–1940 at the state level, not just the Dutch Reformed series (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- For estates, check the Abstracts of Wills series (proved before the Prerogative Court of New York) published by the New-York Historical Society, cited in the same wiki search result.
- Use militia rolls and tax assessment lists as census substitutes for this pre-1790 period (same wiki search result, "Tax and Military Records" section).
- This survey's `wiki_read` calls for `New_York_City_Vital_Records` and `New_York_Vital_Records` both returned a generic, non-jurisdiction-specific "Genealogy_Records" page rather than a 404 or an actual dedicated page — treat the vital-records start date as unconfirmed by the FamilySearch Wiki rather than assuming none exists; consider trying the FamilySearch Wiki directly in a browser.
- The FamilySearch Catalog (`catalog_search`) returned zero hits for both "New York, New York, United States" and "New York, United States" — this is a cataloguing gap in the tool used, not evidence the underlying manuscripts don't exist; a direct catalog search on FamilySearch's website is advisable.

---
I looked at New York City's records from the 1700s, when it was a British colonial port city that had earlier been the Dutch town of New Amsterdam. Because there was no government birth/marriage/death registration back then, the main substitutes are church records — especially the Dutch Reformed congregation's registers, which survive as unsearchable Dutch-language page images that must be read one by one rather than searched by name, plus Anglican and Presbyterian church registers. Wills, land records, tax lists, and militia rolls are the other strong sources for this era, with will abstracts published by the New-York Historical Society and various colonial collections also held by the New York Genealogical & Biographical Society, though this search could not pin down exactly what is available on paper there or in any other physical archive. One important caution: standard genealogy search tools returned only generic, non-specific guidance pages for New York's vital records and had no catalog listings at all for this place and period, so quite a bit here remains to be checked directly on the FamilySearch website or in person.

Next, you may want to give me a specific ancestor name and approximate date so I can search within the Dutch Reformed Church register images and the church/probate/land collections identified above, or ask me to build a research plan for that person.

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- Virginia became a state in 1776 upon declaring independence; prior to that it was a colony.
- Richmond served as the state's seat of government during the war.
- Virginia contributed more troops to the Continental Army than any other colony, and major battles — including Yorktown — were fought on Virginia soil.
- **Important loss:** Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed in the 1814 burning of Washington, D.C. records. County tax lists from the 1780s are the standard substitute.

---

## Military Records — The Core Source Type

| Record Type | Where Held | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Continental Line service records & muster rolls (RG 93) | National Archives (NARA) | archives.gov |
| Pension & bounty-land warrant application files (RG 15) | National Archives (NARA) | archives.gov |
| Virginia militia records | Library of Virginia, Richmond | In-person / by request |
| Virginia State Navy records | Virginia State Library | In-person / mail |
| **FamilySearch:** Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (id 1945678, ~345,678 people, indexed) | FamilySearch.org | Free |

> **Tip:** Pension and bounty-land warrant files (NARA RG 15) often contain the richest genealogical detail — ages, residences, and family members — and are worth checking even when a muster-roll entry has already been found.

---

## Land Records — Bounty Warrants for Veterans

- Virginia granted land bounty warrants to Revolutionary War veterans, with warrant and survey records held at the **Virginia State Library**.
- A digitized browse-only volume of Virginia bounty warrants, 1779–1800 (FamilySearch image group 005301447, 341 images), is available online but is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed image by image.
- The broader **FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900"** (id 1734285, ~2.5 million people) is indexed and covers the war years.

---

## Tax Records — Substitute for the Missing Census

Because the 1790 census was destroyed, **county personal property and land tax lists from the 1780s** are the primary substitute for locating families around that time:
- **FamilySearch:** "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (id 1456723, indexed)
- **Browse-only digitized volume:** State enumerations / tax lists, 1782–1799 (image group 005301449, full-text searchable, not name-indexed)

---

## Court & Probate Records

- **FamilySearch:** "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920" (id 2134567, ~1.7 million people)
- **FamilySearch:** "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (id 1734285)
- A specific browse-only volume of **Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795** (image group 005301448, 158 images) is only 61% name-searchable — most pages must be browsed by image.

---

## Church Records

- **FamilySearch:** "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929" (id 1598230, ~1.2 million people) overlaps the entire war period.
- No civil vital registration existed in Virginia during this era; church registers are the primary substitute for births and deaths.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Role | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Indexed military, land, church, court, and tax records for Virginia | Free |
| National Archives (archives.gov) | Federal military service records and pension files | Free / by request |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records aggregator | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery/burial records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Wartime notices, casualty reports | Subscription |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records |
| Virginia State Library | Bounty-land warrant and survey records |
| County courthouses | Original court order books, deeds, wills |

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Search tax lists first** (1782–1850 on FamilySearch) as a stand-in for the destroyed 1790 census.
2. **Check both NARA record groups** — Continental Line service records (RG 93) and pension/bounty-land files (RG 15) are separate record systems.
3. **Request militia records** from the Library of Virginia directly, as militia service was a state-level (not federal) system.
4. **Browse unindexed volumes by image** for Augusta County court orders and the Revolutionary War land bounty warrants — name searches will not find entries in those volumes.
5. If you have a **specific county**, a county-level guide can identify the parent-county record trail and any local boundary changes.

---

If you have a specific ancestor's name, county, or type of service in mind, I can build a focused research plan or search the military and land record collections directly.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Louisiana (1800-1830)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Founded by the French in 1718; passed to Spain in 1763, briefly back to France, then to the United States via the Louisiana Purchase in 1803; Louisiana became a state in 1812.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans is itself the seat of Orleans Parish.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Louisiana, United States.
- **Economy:** Port and trade city; civil-law legal tradition (Napoleonic Code) rather than English common law, which shapes record types (notarial acts, successions, tutorships, interdictions rather than deeds/wills in the common-law sense).
- **Ethnic composition:** French and Spanish colonial populations, free people of color, enslaved people, and growing Anglo-American population after 1803 (per Wikipedia).
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral) was dominant through this period.
- **Key historical events:** Fires in 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records; the Louisiana Purchase (1803) transferred the territory to the US; repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes and floods further damaged archival holdings (per Wikipedia and FamilySearch Wiki).

## Boundary changes
- Louisiana Territory became the State of Louisiana in 1812; New Orleans and Orleans Parish boundaries were not reported as changing within 1800-1830 by the tools consulted.
- Records from the colonial (French/Spanish) period before 1803 were created under those governments and are held separately from later US-era civil records (see Notarial Archives, below).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The Louisiana Statewide Death Index collection begins in 1819 (collections_search), but this is a derivative index, not proof statewide civil registration began that year; the Louisiana_Vital_Records wiki page could not be resolved to jurisdiction-specific content in this survey, so the exact registration level and start year are not confirmed here.
- **What exists:** No indexed civil birth/marriage records specific to 1800-1830 were returned; a death index collection (1819-1964) was found.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge, per FamilySearch Wiki search result.
- **Gaps:** Civil vital registration appears limited or absent for this early period; church sacramental registers are the primary substitute (see below).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral) dominant in this period.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731 (with gaps), per FamilySearch Wiki search result (New Orleans Genealogy, 'Records Surviving Disasters').
- **Where held:** Parish/archdiocesan archives; also appears in FamilySearch's "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" collection (id 1612905, 987,654 persons, collections_search).
- **Gaps:** Pre-1794 registers may be incomplete owing to the 1788 and 1794 fires; exact loss extent not stated by any tool result consulted.
- **Language:** French and Spanish for the colonial period; collection volume 004990115 (notarial, 1803-1820) is noted in French and English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Louisiana joined the US in 1812; the earliest federal census covering it as a state is 1820 (1810 Louisiana census exists per national pattern, not independently confirmed by a tool result here).
- **State/provincial census:** Not confirmed by tools consulted.
- **Access:** Not detailed by collections_search or volume_search results for this place/period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Successions (Louisiana's civil-law equivalent of probate), tutorships (guardianship), interdictions.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch's "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" collection (id 2078341, 456,789 persons) covers this period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana courts and the Louisiana State Archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system and land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not stated by any tool result in this survey.
- **Types:** Notarial acts record most property transactions in this civil-law jurisdiction rather than county-style deeds.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734, per FamilySearch Wiki search result); a browse-only FamilySearch microfilm volume of notarial acts, 1803-1820 (image group 004990115, 167 images, French/English, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable) also exists.

### Military records
- Not detailed by tool results for this place/period; the War of 1812 (including the 1815 Battle of New Orleans) falls in this window and NARA-held service/pension files are the standard national source, per the generic FamilySearch guide consulted.

### Cemetery records
- Not detailed by any tool result for this place/period; no FindAGrave-specific New Orleans data returned.

### Newspaper records
- Not detailed by any tool result in this survey.

### Immigration/emigration records
- New Orleans was a major port of entry in this period; passenger lists and naturalization records would be expected at NARA, but no place-specific collection was returned by the tools consulted.

### Tax records
- Not detailed by any tool result in this survey.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (987,654 persons); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957 (1,135,780 persons); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (456,789 persons); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (2,345,678 persons) | Substitutes for missing early civil vital and probate records | Free |

The bulk of the Notarial Archives' 30+ million pages are not digitized online per the tool results consulted; only one browse-only microfilm volume (1803-1820) was found in volume_search. The FamilySearch Wiki search result states that the 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records; it does not specify which exact record series were lost versus merely damaged, so this guide reports the loss as stated by that source without narrowing it to a specific record type. - Search Louisiana's civil-law record types by their own names - successions, tutorships, interdictions - rather than assuming county-style wills and guardianship dockets (FamilySearch Wiki, Louisiana Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System).
- The one FamilySearch microfilm volume covering 1803-1820 notarial acts for this place (image group 004990115) is 0% indexed and not full-text searchable - it must be browsed image by image, and is partly in French.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Louisiana (1800-1830)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Founded by the French in 1718; passed to Spain in 1763, briefly back to France, then to the United States via the Louisiana Purchase in 1803; Louisiana became a state in 1812.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans is itself the seat of Orleans Parish.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Louisiana, United States.
- **Economy:** Port and trade city; civil-law legal tradition (Napoleonic Code) rather than English common law, which shapes record types (notarial acts, successions, tutorships, interdictions rather than deeds/wills in the common-law sense).
- **Ethnic composition:** French and Spanish colonial populations, free people of color, enslaved people, and growing Anglo-American population after 1803 (per Wikipedia).
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral) was dominant through this period.
- **Key historical events:** Fires in 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records; the Louisiana Purchase (1803) transferred the territory to the US; repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes and floods further damaged archival holdings (per Wikipedia and FamilySearch Wiki).

## Boundary changes
- Louisiana Territory became the State of Louisiana in 1812; New Orleans and Orleans Parish boundaries were not reported as changing within 1800-1830 by the tools consulted.
- Records from the colonial (French/Spanish) period before 1803 were created under those governments and are held separately from later US-era civil records (see Notarial Archives, below).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The Louisiana Statewide Death Index collection begins in 1819 (collections_search), but this is a derivative index, not proof statewide civil registration began that year; the Louisiana_Vital_Records wiki page could not be resolved to jurisdiction-specific content in this survey, so the exact registration level and start year are not confirmed here.
- **What exists:** No indexed civil birth/marriage records specific to 1800-1830 were returned; a death index collection (1819-1964) was found.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge, per FamilySearch Wiki search result.
- **Gaps:** Civil vital registration appears limited or absent for this early period; church sacramental registers are the primary substitute (see below).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral) dominant in this period.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731 (with gaps), per FamilySearch Wiki search result (New Orleans Genealogy, 'Records Surviving Disasters').
- **Where held:** Parish/archdiocesan archives; also appears in FamilySearch's "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" collection (id 1612905, 987,654 persons, collections_search).
- **Gaps:** Pre-1794 registers may be incomplete owing to the 1788 and 1794 fires; exact loss extent not stated by any tool result consulted.
- **Language:** French and Spanish for the colonial period; collection volume 004990115 (notarial, 1803-1820) is noted in French and English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Louisiana joined the US in 1812; the earliest federal census covering it as a state is 1820 (1810 Louisiana census exists per national pattern, not independently confirmed by a tool result here).
- **State/provincial census:** Not confirmed by tools consulted.
- **Access:** Not detailed by collections_search or volume_search results for this place/period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Successions (Louisiana's civil-law equivalent of probate), tutorships (guardianship), interdictions.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch's "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" collection (id 2078341, 456,789 persons) covers this period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana courts and the Louisiana State Archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system and land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not stated by any tool result in this survey.
- **Types:** Notarial acts record most property transactions in this civil-law jurisdiction rather than county-style deeds.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734, per FamilySearch Wiki search result); a browse-only FamilySearch microfilm volume of notarial acts, 1803-1820 (image group 004990115, 167 images, French/English, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable) also exists.

### Military records
- Not detailed by tool results for this place/period; the War of 1812 (including the 1815 Battle of New Orleans) falls in this window and NARA-held service/pension files are the standard national source, per the generic FamilySearch guide consulted.

### Cemetery records
- Not detailed by any tool result for this place/period; no FindAGrave-specific New Orleans data returned.

### Newspaper records
- Not detailed by any tool result in this survey.

### Immigration/emigration records
- New Orleans was a major port of entry in this period; passenger lists and naturalization records would be expected at NARA, but no place-specific collection was returned by the tools consulted.

### Tax records
- Not detailed by any tool result in this survey.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (987,654 persons); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957 (1,135,780 persons); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (456,789 persons); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (2,345,678 persons) | Substitutes for missing early civil vital and probate records | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection | General census coverage | Subscription |
| FamilySearch Wiki | Vital Records category page | General reference | Free |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (general site, not place-specific results returned) | Cemetery records gap | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (general site, not place-specific results returned) | Newspaper records gap | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (general site, not place-specific results returned) | Military records gap | Subscription |
| National Archives (NARA) | Federal records generally | Immigration, naturalization, military gaps | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** Only one digitized volume (image group 004990115) matched New Orleans/Orleans Parish for 1800-1820 in volume_search; it is browse-only. The FamilySearch Catalog returned zero hits for this place in this search (a cataloguing gap, not evidence records don't exist).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person; some microfilm reproduced by FamilySearch |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and early state records | In-person / written request |
| St. Louis Cathedral / Archdiocese of New Orleans archives | Sacramental registers from 1731 | Contact archive directly |

## Records NOT online
The bulk of the Notarial Archives' 30+ million pages are not digitized online per the tool results consulted; only one browse-only microfilm volume (1803-1820) was found in volume_search. Probate/succession records beyond the single indexed FamilySearch collection, and any surviving pre-1794 civil records, were not shown as digitized by any tool result in this survey.

## Known record losses
The FamilySearch Wiki search result states that the 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records; it does not specify which exact record series were lost versus merely damaged, so this guide reports the loss as stated by that source without narrowing it to a specific record type. No tool result in this survey stated that the St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers or the notarial archive were destroyed; both are described as surviving (with the sacramental registers having gaps).

## Research tips
- Because of the 1788 and 1794 fires, treat St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731) as the primary substitute for missing early civil vital records (FamilySearch Wiki, New Orleans Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center's over 30 million pages of notarial acts (from 1734) are a major substitute source for property, family, and legal relationships when vital or probate records are missing (same source as above).
- Search Louisiana's civil-law record types by their own names - successions, tutorships, interdictions - rather than assuming county-style wills and guardianship dockets (FamilySearch Wiki, Louisiana Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System).
- The one FamilySearch microfilm volume covering 1803-1820 notarial acts for this place (image group 004990115) is 0% indexed and not full-text searchable - it must be browsed image by image, and is partly in French.
- The FamilySearch Wiki getting-started, online-records, research-tips, and Vital Records pages could not be retrieved as Louisiana-specific content in this survey (they returned only a generic templated page); treat the registration-start date and record-availability claims above as unconfirmed rather than assuming the generic page's dates apply to Louisiana.
- The FamilySearch Catalog returned zero hits for this place; that is a cataloguing gap, not evidence the records don't exist - consult the Louisiana State Archives and Notarial Archives directly.

# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — 1840s Immigration Focus

## Jurisdiction Overview
Boston is a long-established city within Suffolk County, Massachusetts — one of the principal U.S. ports of entry in the 1840s. This decade saw a massive surge of Irish immigration during the Great Famine (1845–1852); by 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born.

---

## Key Record Types for 1840s Boston Immigrants

### 1. Customs Passenger Lists (Primary Source)
- **Series:** National Archives Record Group 36 — "Passenger Lists, Port of Boston," 1820–1891
- **What they record:** Name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin (1840s lists are sparse compared to later Ellis Island–era manifests)
- **Digitized volume found:** Image group **003345210**, covering 1840–1850 (389 images) — only **3% name-indexed** but **full-text searchable**; use keyword/text search, not a name index alone
- **Online collections:**
  - **FamilySearch** collection **1784312**, "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (~1.23M people) — free
  - **Ancestry** also holds indexes/images of this series — subscription required
- **Physical originals:** National Archives at Boston (Waltham) — in-person or written request

### 2. Catholic Parish Registers
- **Why essential:** Civil registration is thin for this period; Catholic church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) are often the only way to reconstruct families after arrival
- **Key parishes:** Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's, which grew rapidly to serve Irish immigrants
- **Where held:** **Archdiocese of Boston Archives**
- **Online:** FamilySearch collection **1921657**, "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" — free

### 3. Naturalization Records
- For post-arrival naturalization — scattered across federal, state, and local courts
- **FamilySearch collection 1459213**, "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" — free

### 4. Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **FamilySearch collection 2061550**, "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" — overlaps this period

### 5. Federal Census Records
- The **1840** and **1850** U.S. federal censuses both fall within this window and are excellent for locating recently arrived families

### 6. Probate Records
- **FamilySearch collection 1678901**, "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991"

### 7. The Pilot (Newspaper)
- Boston's Irish Catholic newspaper published **arrival notices** and **missing-persons advertisements** — invaluable for Famine-era immigrants. Check Newspapers.com or local archives.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Passenger lists, church records, naturalization, vital records | Free |
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham) | Original RG 36 customs passenger lists | In-person / written request |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers | Contact archives directly |
| Ancestry | Census records, passenger list images | Subscription |

---

## Key Research Tips

- **1840s manifests are thin** — only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin. Don't expect birthplace villages or family relationships on these lists.
- **The Port of Boston 1840–1850 digitized volume (image group 003345210) is only 3% name-indexed** — search it by full-text keyword, not by name index.
- **Catholic parish registers are essential** for reconstructing Irish immigrant families alongside (or before) civil records.
- **The Pilot newspaper** is a uniquely valuable resource for Famine-era Irish immigrants seeking or being sought by relatives.

If you'd like, a research plan can be built from this guide to search specific collections for named ancestors.

# Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma (mid-1800s)

## Jurisdiction Overview

The region was designated **Indian Territory** under the Indian Removal Act of 1830, used for the forced relocation of tribal nations. It did not become the State of Oklahoma until 1907. No county-level civil jurisdiction existed there in the mid-1800s — authority ran through tribal governments and federal Indian agencies. The Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole) relocated via the Trail of Tears and governed themselves under federal oversight.

---

## Boundary Notes

Indian Territory was not organized into counties during this period. Researchers should treat **"Indian Territory"** as the operative jurisdiction — not modern Oklahoma counties — for any mid-1800s research.

---

## Available Record Types

### Tribal Rolls & Enrollment Records
- **Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)** and **Drennen Roll (1852)** are the most relevant mid-1800s rolls.
- The later **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** are the most widely used Five Tribes enrollment records (name, age, sex, blood quantum, tribal affiliation) and should be cross-referenced against earlier rolls.
- **Where held:** National Archives at Fort Worth; Dawes Rolls indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Digitized volume confirmed:** FamilySearch image group **002298871** — "Tribal Enrollment Cards," 1840–1870, 940 images, 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable.

### Treaty & Federal Agency Records
- Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) agency records: annuity payment rolls, correspondence, school records.
- **Where held:** National Archives (main and Fort Worth branch).
- Note: FamilySearch catalog searches under "Oklahoma, United States" returned zero hits — search instead under **"Indian Territory,"** specific tribal nation names, or federal agency names.

### Church / Mission Records
- Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missions were active from the 1820s onward.
- **FamilySearch collection confirmed:** "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (~123,456 persons) — covers the mid-1800s window.

### Tribal Censuses
- **FamilySearch collection confirmed:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (~567,890 persons) — directly covers the target period.
- No federal decennial census was taken in Indian Territory in this period.

### Land Records
- **FamilySearch collection confirmed:** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (~234,567 persons).

### Probate & Court Records
- Tribal nations maintained their own courts; no specific digitized collection was confirmed in this survey — treat as likely physical-only until checked with the National Archives or individual tribal archives.

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Not applicable** for the mid-1800s — there was no civil registration in Indian Territory.
- **Substitutes:** Tribal rolls, mission registers, and BIA agency records fill this gap.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Indian Censuses & Rolls 1851–1959; Land Records 1834–1907; Mission & Church Records 1820–1965; Tribal Enrollment Cards 1840–1870 (image group 002298871) | Free |
| Ancestry | Dawes Rolls and related allotment records | Subscription |
| National Archives (archives.gov) | BIA agency originals, annuity rolls, Dawes Roll originals | Free / in-person or request |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| National Archives at Fort Worth | Dawes Rolls, allotment records |
| National Archives (main) | BIA correspondence, annuity rolls, school records |
| Tribal nation archives (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole) | Nation-specific rolls, council and court records — contact each tribe directly |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1851 and 1852 rolls** (Old Settler Cherokee Roll; Drennen Roll) rather than jumping straight to the Dawes Rolls — these are the mid-1800s-specific enrollments.
2. **Cross-reference early rolls with the Dawes Rolls**: because they record blood quantum and tribal affiliation, working both series together reveals family continuity.
3. **BIA annuity payment rolls** often name heads of household or entire families and can substitute for census records in this period.
4. **Mission registers** (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian) may record baptisms, marriages, and deaths decades before any civil registration existed.
5. **Catalog searching tip:** Use "Indian Territory" or specific tribal-nation names rather than "Oklahoma, United States" — the modern state place label returns no catalog hits for this period.
6. **Contact tribal archives directly** for nation-level administrative records (tribal council minutes, court records) not held at the National Archives.

---

## Known Gaps in This Survey
- Oklahoma-specific FamilySearch Wiki guide pages could not be retrieved; visit the FamilySearch Wiki directly for Oklahoma and Indian Territory pages.
- Tribal court and probate records: not confirmed as digitized — assume physical-only until verified.
- No confirmed record of losses for this region, but absence of confirmation is not evidence of completeness.

---

**Bottom line:** Because Indian Territory had no counties or civil vital-records registration in the mid-1800s, tribal enrollment rolls, BIA agency papers, and mission church registers are the core substitutes. The Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and Drennen Roll (1852) are your starting points; FamilySearch hosts confirmed collections for tribal censuses, land records, and mission records; and original federal agency records sit at the National Archives in Fort Worth.

Here is what the locality-guide found for Pennsylvania Quaker research in the late 1700s:

---

**Pennsylvania Quaker Families — Late 1700s Research Guide**

Pennsylvania had **no civil registration** of births, marriages, or deaths until 1906, so for Quaker ancestors the monthly meeting records are the essential substitute. Monthly meetings kept detailed minutes covering:

- **Births and deaths**
- **Marriages** (Friends married within the meeting, with witnesses listed)
- **Certificates of removal** — issued when a family relocated to another meeting; these trace migration across counties and states
- **Disownments** — common during the Revolutionary War period for members who took up arms or swore oaths

The densest Quaker populations in this era were in **Chester County**, **Bucks County**, and **Philadelphia**.

---

**Key Repositories and Resources**

| Resource | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** | The single largest repository of Pennsylvania Quaker meeting records |
| **William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 vols.)** | Widely used published abstracts of meeting minutes — useful when originals aren't digitized |
| **FamilySearch Catalog** | Search directly for specific county meeting records; some Philadelphia Yearly Meeting minutes are digitized but unindexed (must be browsed page by page) |

> **Note:** Searches of the general FamilySearch collections and wiki during this survey returned limited Pennsylvania-specific Quaker results — that reflects a gap in the online lookup, not an absence of surviving records.

---

**Recommended Next Step**

Build a research plan targeting the specific Chester, Bucks, or Philadelphia monthly meeting minutes for your ancestor's location, cross-referencing Hinshaw's abstracts, and following any removal certificates to trace the family as they moved between meetings.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania, United States — Quaker Communities (1750-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States; Pennsylvania as a state dates from 1787 per place_search, though Quaker settlement and meeting structures long predate that.
- **Population during period:** place_population returned no data for this query; not confirmed in this survey.
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers) had dense populations in Chester County, Bucks County, and Philadelphia, per the FamilySearch Wiki's Pennsylvania Church Records page.
- **Key historical events:** This period spans the American Revolution and early Republic; Quaker meetings' pacifist stance led to disownments of members who took up arms or swore oaths, visible in meeting discipline records.

## Boundary changes
- Not surveyed in detail for this theme; Pennsylvania's county structure (Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia) was established well before 1750 and is treated as stable for this guide's purposes.

## Available record types

### Church (Quaker meeting) records
- **What exists:** Monthly meeting minutes recording births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal (transfers between meetings), and disownments (disciplinary proceedings); marriage certificates were signed by all attendees. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Church Records — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records
- **Digitized volume found:** volume_search returned one matching volume for this period: imageGroupNumber 001188322, "Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes," covering Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, 1750-1800, 145 images, 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — classified **browse-only images**, must be paged through image by image.
- **Where held:** The Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College holds the largest collection of American Quaker records, per the FamilySearch Wiki. FamilySearch has microfilmed many monthly meeting minutes and registers (per the same page), and holds the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes volume named above.
- **Published abstracts:** William Wade Hinshaw's Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy (6 volumes) abstracts meeting records from Pennsylvania and other states — a practical finding aid when an original minute book is not digitized. Source: same FamilySearch Wiki page.
- **Gaps:** catalog_search for Pennsylvania with subject "Quakers" returned zero hits in this survey — a cataloguing gap in this tool, not evidence the records are unavailable; search the FamilySearch Catalog directly and consult Swarthmore's Friends Historical Library.
- **Language:** English.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- Pennsylvania had no statewide civil registration requirement until 1906 (per the generic FamilySearch state overview fetched in this survey, which gives this date without naming a level below "statewide"). For 1750-1800, Quaker meeting records substitute for civil vital records.
- collections_search returned "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950" (id 1571957, 624,090 people) and "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900" (id 1502909, 397,530 people), both of which overlap the target period, though neither is Quaker-specific.

### Probate and court records
- collections_search returned "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (id 1999196), overlapping the target period; its personCount came back as 0 in this survey, so indexed-name coverage for 1750-1800 could not be confirmed.
- Quaker meetings sometimes administered their own disciplinary "courts" (meeting for business); county probate and orphans' court records run alongside and should still be checked for wills and estate administrations of Quaker families.

### Repository guide

| Repository | Collections for this theme | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (imageGroupNumber 001188322, browse-only); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950; Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 | Browse-only original minutes; civil-marriage and probate overlap records | Free |
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College | Largest collection of American Quaker meeting records (per FamilySearch Wiki) | Original/microfilmed meeting minutes beyond what FamilySearch has filmed | Physical/by request |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned exactly one matching digitized volume for Pennsylvania, 1750-1800, in the Religious record-type groups queried; it is reported in full above, not a partial page.

## Records NOT online
- The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes volume (001188322) is online as images only, with 0% name indexing and no full-text search — it must be browsed page by page.
- Monthly meeting minutes for Chester County and Bucks County meetings were not returned by volume_search or collections_search in this survey; check the FamilySearch Catalog and Swarthmore's Friends Historical Library directly for their holdings.

## Known record losses
- No tool result in this survey reported destroyed or lost Quaker meeting records for Pennsylvania; none is claimed here.

## Research tips
- Search monthly meeting minutes for births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal, and disownments — a certificate of removal tracks a family's move between meetings and can connect two localities. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Church Records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records).
- Consult William Wade Hinshaw's Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy (6 volumes) as a finding aid/abstract before searching an unindexed original minute book. Same source.
- Prioritize Chester County, Bucks County, and Philadelphia monthly meetings, the densest Quaker population centers named in this period by the FamilySearch Wiki. Same source.
- Because the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes volume is 0% indexed and not full-text searchable, plan to browse it image by image rather than relying on a name search.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's generic state-level pages (overview, getting started, online records, research tips) returned only boilerplate U.S.-state content for Pennsylvania in this survey, with no Quaker-specific detail — rely on the Pennsylvania Church Records page instead for this theme.
- Treat a zero-hit catalog_search or an empty collections_search row (such as the Probate Records collection's personCount of 0) as a coverage gap in this survey, not proof the records do not exist — check the FamilySearch Catalog and Swarthmore's Friends Historical Library directly.

loc_001 recorded for Pennsylvania, United States, covering Quaker communities 1750-1800.

---

Pennsylvania Quaker families from the late 1700s are best traced through Quaker monthly meeting records rather than civil records, since Pennsylvania had no statewide birth, marriage, or death registration until 1906. Monthly meetings (local Quaker congregations) kept detailed minutes of births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal when a family moved between meetings, and disownments when a member was expelled for breaking Quaker discipline (common during the Revolutionary War for taking up arms or swearing oaths); the densest Quaker populations were in Chester County, Bucks County, and Philadelphia. The single largest known repository is the Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College, and William Wade Hinshaw's six-volume Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy is a widely used published abstract of these minutes when the originals aren't digitized; one digitized volume of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting minutes from this period was found online but only as unindexed images that must be browsed page by page, not searched by name. Searches of the general FamilySearch catalog for "Quakers" and of the general Pennsylvania wiki overview pages came back empty or only generic in this survey, which is a gap in this particular lookup rather than proof the records don't exist, so a direct visit to Swarthmore's library catalog and the FamilySearch Catalog is still worthwhile.

The next step would be to build a research plan that works through specific Chester, Bucks, and Philadelphia monthly meeting minutes and the Hinshaw abstracts to identify the ancestor's meeting and trace the family across any removal certificates.

Here is the locality guide produced for **Pittsburgh / Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, 1870–1900**:

---

## Pittsburgh — Tracing Families Through Occupational & Industrial Sources

The late 1800s steel boom drew waves of Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian mill workers into Allegheny County. Tracing them requires layering several record types rather than relying on a single source:

### Federal Census Records
- **1880 and 1900 censuses** record occupation and (in 1900) immigration year — the two most useful snapshots for steel-era workers.

### City Directories
- **Pittsburgh city directories**, held at the **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh**, can track a worker's job, employer, and address year by year between census years. This is often the best way to follow a family through the boom decades.

### Church (Parish) Records
- **Catholic parish baptism, marriage, and burial registers** are essential for immigrant families. These are held by the **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives**. Knowing the ethnic parish (Irish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, etc.) is key to finding the right register.

### Naturalization Records
- **Pre-1906 naturalization records** are held at the **National Archives — Mid-Atlantic Region (Philadelphia)**. These often name country/town of origin, the single most valuable fact for tracing immigrants back to Europe.

### Industrial & Union Collections
- The **Heinz History Center (Senator John Heinz History Center)** holds company records, union membership lists, and immigration collections built specifically around the Pittsburgh steel workforce — a unique repository for occupational research.

---

### Important Caveats
- Many of the most useful records (parish registers, mill employment files, union lists, city directories) **exist only on paper in physical archives**, not online. Plan for a visit or written request to these repositories.
- Online genealogy databases for this area generally cover Pennsylvania at the whole-state level, not Allegheny County specifically, so broad name searches may be needed.

---

### Suggested Next Steps
1. **Identify your ancestor's specific occupation and employer** (steel mill, coke works, iron foundry) — this narrows which company/union records to request.
2. **Identify the ethnic community and parish** to target the right church register.
3. Build a research plan targeting these repositories in sequence, starting with the 1880 and 1900 censuses to establish the household baseline.

# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1870-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County formed 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland counties (FamilySearch Wiki, 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy').
- **County seat:** Pittsburgh.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States.
- **Population during period:** place_population returned no data for this place/period in this run - not confirmed by this survey.
- **Economy:** Pittsburgh became the center of the American steel industry in the late 1800s (Andrew Carnegie's steel empire and other major firms) (Wikipedia, 'Pittsburgh').
- **Ethnic composition:** Massive immigration of Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers to the mills (Wikipedia, 'Pittsburgh').
- **Religious denominations:** Many ethnic Catholic parishes (Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish) from the 1840s onward (FamilySearch Wiki, 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy').
- **Key historical events:** Rise of Carnegie's steel empire and associated labor immigration waves in the late 1800s (Wikipedia, 'Pittsburgh').

## Boundary changes
This survey found no record of boundary changes to Allegheny County or Pittsburgh during 1870-1900; place_search/place_search_all were not run for historical boundary variants because none were indicated.

- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church (parish) baptism, marriage, and burial registers from the 1840s onward.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Ethnic Catholic parishes - Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish - from the 1840s onward (FamilySearch Wiki, 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy').
- **Record types:** Baptism, marriage, and burial registers.
- **Where held:** The Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives holds many originals.
- **Gaps:** This survey did not confirm online digitization of these parish registers; collections_search did not return a Pittsburgh-specific parish collection (it returned only Pennsylvania-state-level collections).
- **Language:** Records for ethnic parishes may be in languages other than English (e.g., Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian); this survey did not confirm specifics.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Federal census records for Allegheny County survive from 1800; the 1880 and 1900 censuses are especially valuable for industrial workers, recording occupation, parents' birthplace, and (1900) immigration year (FamilySearch Wiki, 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy').
- **State/provincial census:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Other enumerations:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Access:** This survey did not confirm indexing status for the 1880/1900 Allegheny County census; volume_search returned no county-specific census volumes.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, administrations, guardianship files.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not established for any specific ancestor in this survey; search both wills and administrations.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch's 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' (collection 1999196, person_count 0 - i.e., unindexed) spans this period; volume_search found a matching browse-only probate volume (image group 008120441, 1,180 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Where held:** County courthouse originals; FamilySearch holds a browse-only digitized volume (no name index).

- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not confirmed by this survey - the {Jurisdiction}_Land_and_Property wiki page was not reached (place_page sections returned only generic content).

- **Record types:** Not detailed by this run's tool results.
- **Where held:** National Archives (NARA), per external_links_search result.

- **Major cemeteries:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/), per external_links_search.
- **Physical records:** Not confirmed by this survey.

- **Local papers:** Not named by this survey.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/), per external_links_search.
- **Content value:** Obituaries and marriage notices likely, not separately confirmed.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Pittsburgh is inland; immigrants to the steel mills typically arrived via East Coast ports (not specified by this run's tool results) and then migrated inland.
- **Record types:** Naturalization petitions - Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalization records (1798-1930) are held at the National Archives at Philadelphia (FamilySearch Wiki, 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy'). volume_search also found a Pennsylvania-level naturalization volume (image group 008120443, 351 images, 15% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, in English and German).
